drafts.title: Dinner is coming. What’s in the fridge?
drafts.body:
It’s 5:30. Everybody’s hungry. The fridge has eggs, rice and half a bag of carrots.

Try asking AI: “Give me three easy dinners with these ingredients. No extra shopping.”

Check the suggestions, then pick one.

What would you ask it to make with your leftovers?
bullets: Suggested everyday AI prompt using a hypothetical pantry. No personal experience or guaranteed result is claimed. Review suggestions for suitability.

drafts.title: Would an EV fit your Tuesday?
drafts.body:
School drop-off. Work. Groceries. Home.

That’s the EV question worth asking: can you charge where you park and cover your usual day?

A home charger isn’t an option for everybody. If you’d rely on public charging, check the stops and prices first.

What would work for you?
bullets: An opinion and practical charging checklist, not a claim that EVs fit every household. DOE describes home and public charging considerations. No personal ownership story is implied.

drafts.title: Same car. Different charging bill.
drafts.body:
An EV charging timer is worth a look before bed.

At 15¢ per kWh, 40 kWh costs $6. At 30¢, it’s $12. Same amount of electricity.

Those are example rates. Check your utility’s actual plan, including peak-hour costs for the rest of the house.

Does yours offer cheaper nights?
bullets: Illustrative arithmetic, not current local rates or promised savings: 40 × $0.15 = $6; 40 × $0.30 = $12. DOE confirms some utilities offer time-of-use rates. Compare the entire household tariff.
